content: Monoterpenes are a class of terpenes composed of two isoprene units, resulting in the molecular formula C10H16. These compounds can exist in either linear (acyclic) forms or as structures containing rings. Through biochemical modifications such as oxidation or molecular rearrangement, monoterpenes can be converted into related compounds known as monoterpenoids. Acyclic Monoterpenes In the biosynthesis of acyclic monoterpenes, isopentenyl pyrophosphate and dimethylallyl pyrophosphate combine to form geranyl pyrophosphate. The removal of the pyrophosphate group from geranyl pyrophosphate leads to the formation of acyclic monoterpenes, such as ocimene and myrcene. Hydrolysis of the phosphate groups results in the production of geraniol, which is considered the prototypical acyclic monoterpenoid. Further rearrangements and oxidation reactions yield compounds such as citral, citronellal, citronellol, linalool, and many others. Additionally, many monoterpenes found in marine organisms are halogenated, with halomon being a notable example. Monocyclic Monoterpenes In addition to linear structures, isoprene units can form connections that result in ring structures. Among monoterpenes, the most common ring size is a six-membered ring. A classic example of this is the cyclization of geranyl pyrophosphate to produce limonene. Similarly, compounds such as the terpinene isomers, phellandrenes, and terpinolene are formed through comparable cyclization processes. Hydroxylation of these compounds, followed by dehydration, can lead to the formation of aromatic compounds like p-cymene. Important terpenoids derived from monocyclic monoterpenes include menthol, thymol, carvacrol, and several others. Bicyclic Monoterpenes Geranyl pyrophosphate can also undergo two sequential cyclization reactions to form bicyclic monoterpenes. A prominent example is pinene, which is the primary constituent of pine resin. Other bicyclic monoterpenes include carene, sabinene, camphene, and thujene. Bicyclic monoterpenoids, such as camphor, borneol, and eucalyptol, are characterized by the presence of functional groups like ketones, alcohols, and ethers, respectively.
